events.title: Formalisation of the eco‑village movement

events.title: Research on ecovillages by Judit Farkas
events.description: Judit Farkas began studying ecovillages in 2008, focusing on the socio‑cultural dimensions of the eco‑village movement and its relationship to broader environmental and migration processes.
events.supporting_text: The author of this article studies ecovillages since 2008.

significance.justification: Provides scholarly insight that can guide practitioners and policy‑makers.
significance.supporting_text: author of this article studies ecovillages since 2008

events.title: Publication of Karen Litfin's 2011 work on the eco‑village movement
events.description: A scholarly work by political scientist Karen Litfin that discusses the eco‑village movement, cited in the text (Litfin 2011:139).
events.supporting_text: This sentence was written by Karen Litfin, a political scientist, researcher of the international eco‑village movement (Litfin 2011:139).

significance.justification: Litfin’s analysis diagnoses societal problems through eco‑village values, highlighting current disharmony.
significance.supporting_text: “the investigation of the set of values in an eco‑village … might reflect a proper diagnosis to the problems of our current society” (Litfin 2011:139).

events.title: Student protest at University of Copenhagen natural sciences class
events.description: In the spring of 1969 a group of University of Copenhagen students interrupted a natural sciences lecture, entered the room carrying a mallard that had been soaked in a marine oil spill, and recited anti‑pollution slogans, exemplifying the radicalisation of the emerging environmental movement.
events.supporting_text: in the Spring of 1969 a couple of students interrupted the class on natural sciences at the University of Copenhagen, rushing in, carrying a mallard soaked in a marine oil spill and reciting anti-pollution slogans.

significance.justification: Shows grassroots mobilization against pollution, illustrating collective agency.
significance.supporting_text: students interrupted the class ... carrying a mallard soaked in a marine oil spill and reciting anti‑pollution slogans

significance.supporting_text: The first Kibbutz was founded in 1909 and the related movement (United Kibbutz Movement) was formed in 1927.

events.title: Formation of United Kibbutz Movement

events.title: Establishment of Findhorn Foundation
events.description: Findhorn Foundation was established in Scotland, later becoming a leading eco‑village community.
events.supporting_text: One of the best known such community building on a life close to nature and nature related spiritual values was the Findhorn Foundation established in 1962 Scotland.

significance.justification: Creates a long‑standing intentional community that serves as a practical hub for ecological regeneration.
significance.supporting_text: One of the best known such community ... was the Findhorn Foundation established in 1962 Scotland.

events.title: Mother Earth News sets up organic gardens and energy‑saving houses
events.description: Mother Earth News magazine started setting up organic gardens and energy‑saving houses next to its offices, functioning as education centres.
events.supporting_text: According to a historian of the eco‑village movement (Bates 2003) the magazine called Mother Earth News (Hendersonville, North‑California) started to set up organic gardens and energy saving houses next to their offices in 1975.

significance.justification: Demonstrates concrete sustainable practices that can be replicated by others.
significance.supporting_text: Mother Earth News ... started to set up organic gardens and energy saving houses next to their offices in 1975, which also functioned as education centres.

events.title: Mother Earth News adopts the term “eco‑village”
events.description: The magazine began referring to its sites as eco‑villages.
events.supporting_text: and they started to call themselves eco‑village from 1979 on.

significance.justification: Introduces and popularises the label that frames the movement in public discourse.
significance.supporting_text: they started to call themselves eco‑village from 1979 on.

events.title: First eco‑village meeting in Denmark
events.description: A meeting held in Denmark aimed to define an eco‑village concept and formulate a propagation strategy.
events.supporting_text: The first such meeting was held in Denmark in 1991, with the aim to define an eco‑village concept and to formulate a strategy of propagation.

significance.justification: Brings together disparate initiatives to coordinate and define a shared vision.
significance.supporting_text: The first such meeting was held in Denmark in 1991, with the aim to define an eco‑village concept and to formulate a strategy of propagation.

events.title: Establishment of Danish eco‑village network
events.description: The Danish eco‑village network was set up, becoming a model for later international eco‑village initiatives.
events.supporting_text: In 1993 the Danish eco‑village network was set up, the first of this kind, which later served as a model for the later launched international eco‑village movement.

significance.justification: Creates a national network that enables knowledge exchange and joint action.
significance.supporting_text: In 1993 the Danish eco‑village network was set up, the first of this kind.

events.title: Launch of Global Ecovillage Network (GEN)
events.description: The international Global Ecovillage Network was launched, with the Hungarian Gyűrűfű project participating as a funding member.
events.supporting_text: The international network, Global Ecovillage Network (GEN) was launched in 1994, in which the Hungarian Gyűrűfű project has already been involved as one of the funding members.

significance.justification: Establishes a global platform that can catalyse systemic transformation toward sustainability.
significance.supporting_text: The international network, Global Ecovillage Network (GEN) was launched in 1994.

events.title: First international eco‑village meeting in Findhorn, Scotland
events.description: An international eco‑village meeting titled “Ecovillages and Sustainable Communities. Models for the 21st Century” was held in Findhorn, organized by Gaia Trust and the Findhorn Foundation.
events.supporting_text: The first international eco‑village meeting took place in 1995 in Findhorn, Scotland, organised and sponsored by the Gaia Trust and the Findhorn Foundation. The title of the event ‒ Ecovillages and Sustainable Communities. Models for the 21st Century ‒ formulated and marked out the road precisely on which eco‑villages intend to walk.

significance.justification: Gives the movement high‑profile international visibility and legitimacy.
significance.supporting_text: The first international eco‑village meeting took place in 1995 in Findhorn, Scotland, organised and sponsored by the Gaia Trust and the Findhorn Foundation.

events.title: 1960s wave of intentional communities
events.description: A huge wave of intentional communities emerged from the counterculture of the 1960s, with more than 2,000 communities founded, many motivated by resistance to consumerism and a desire for freedom.
events.supporting_text: the seventh phase in the 1960s brought a huge wave of intentional communities surfacing from the counterculture of the period, in the United States of America alone, more than 2000 communities were founded at this time.

significance.justification: Shows a cultural shift that opened space for alternative, nature‑centric ways of living.
significance.supporting_text: the seventh phase in the 1960s brought a huge wave of intentional communities surfacing from the counterculture of the period.

events.title: Eighth stage of eco‑village development (late 1990s onward)
events.description: From the end of the 1990s, intentional communities have been divided into cohousing and eco‑villages, with growth of spiritually and environmentally conscious settlements.
events.supporting_text: Finally, Meijering dates the eighth stage from the end of the 1990s, within which period the communities established can be divided into two distinct types: cohousing and eco‑villages.

significance.justification: Identifies the emergence of cohousing and eco‑villages as new systemic pathways.
significance.supporting_text: the eighth stage from the end of the 1990s ... the communities established can be divided into two distinct types: cohousing and eco‑villages.

events.title: 1970s environmental movement strengthening and emergence of eco‑village initiatives
events.description: Environmental movements gained strength and new methods, leading to the first eco‑village initiatives and the appearance of the term “eco‑village”.
events.supporting_text: In the 1970s, thus, the environmental movements have gained strength and acquired new methods on one hand, while community building manifested in new experiments on the other. The first eco‑village initiatives emerged against this social background. The term itself appeared back in the 1970s, but did not gain wide recognition at the time.

significance.justification: Links a broader environmental surge to the birth of eco‑village experiments.
significance.supporting_text: In the 1970s, thus, the environmental movements have gained strength ... the first eco‑village initiatives emerged against this social background.

events.title: 1970s co‑housing movement in Denmark
events.description: The co‑housing movement began to blossom in Denmark.

significance.supporting_text: Also at this time, in the 1970s, the co‑housing movement started to blossom in Denmark.

events.title: Mid‑1990s internet‑facilitated spread of eco‑village ideas
events.description: The rise of affordable internet and the World Wide Web enabled wider outreach for the Global Ecovillage Network, facilitating propagation of eco‑village patterns.
events.supporting_text: The internet, gaining ground at this time, assisted in the spread of the ecovillage idea and hence, the set up of a number of eco‑villages to a great extent: this is the period, when computers and the world wide web have become affordable and accessible for more and more people, allowing a wide outreach for GEN through its web site, facilitating the propagation of the movement and transfer of eco‑village patterns.

significance.justification: Shows how digital connectivity amplified the movement’s reach and scaling potential.
significance.supporting_text: the internet, gaining ground at this time, assisted in the spread of the ecovillage idea ... allowing a wide outreach for GEN through its web site.

events.title: Publication of Robert Gilman's definition of ecovillage
events.description: Robert Gilman first articulated a widely‑used definition of an ecovillage, describing it as a human‑scale, full‑featured settlement that integrates human activities harmlessly into the natural world.
events.supporting_text: "The first attempt at a definition, and still the one most commonly used, is Robert Gilman's: 'A human-scale, full-featured settlement, in which human activities are harmlessly integrated into the natural world …' (1991: 10)."

significance.justification: The definition provides a widely‑cited framing that raises the visibility and legitimacy of ecovillages.
significance.supporting_text: The first attempt at a definition, and still the one most commonly used, is Robert Gilman’s: “A human‑scale, full‑featured settlement…

events.title: Addition of qualification to Gilman's ecovillage definition
events.description: Gilman later qualified his definition, stating that ecovillages should also have multiple centers of initiative such as governance structures, autonomous enterprises, associations, and resident projects.
events.supporting_text: "He added a later qualification in 1999 that ecovillages should also have 'multiple centers of initiative,' including governance structures, autonomous enterprises, associations, and projects of its residents…"

significance.justification: The qualification refines the concept, further shaping discourse and acceptance of ecovillages.
significance.supporting_text: He added a later qualification in 1999 that ecovillages should also have “multiple centers of initiative,”...

events.title: Publication of Dawson's five defining characteristics of ecovillages
events.description: Dawson proposed a more precise definition of ecovillages consisting of five characteristics: private citizens' initiatives, a central communitarian impulse, control over community resources, a strong shared values base (often spiritual), and functioning as centers of research, demonstration and training.
events.supporting_text: "Subsequently, I offered the following five defining characteristics of ecovillages: '[p]rivate citizens' initiatives; ... that have a strong shared values base, often referred to as "spirituality"; and that act as centers of research, demonstration and in most cases training' (Dawson 2006)."

significance.justification: Offers a more precise articulation that helps stakeholders understand and legitimize ecovillages.

events.description: Rural development agencies have, over recent decades, adopted more holistic and integrated community‑driven strategies that were pioneered by ecovillages such as Sarvodaya, blurring the line between ecovillages and conventional rural development initiatives.
